articles.title: Product
articles.content:
We’re introducingGPT-6.1 Terra, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.

Terra continues to advance the cost-intelligence frontier across our model families, providing a new balance of speed, capability, and cost. Its standard API prices are 50% lower than those of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, making it practical for developers to automate high-volume work, like reading incoming invoices and entering their details into accounting software. In ChatGPT Work and Codex, your plan goes further with GPT-6.1 Terra—the same usage allowance covers more tasks than with GPT‑5.6 Terra and substantially more than with GPT‑6.1 Sol or GPT‑6 Astra.

We measured GPT-6.1 Terra’s computer-use capabilities onAgents’ Last Exam,a benchmark of professional tasks that includes turning architectural drawings into a 3D model and reviewing an animated film shot by shot to create a time-coded log for a restoration team. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra scores 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra at about one-third the cost. It even performs on par with GPT-6 Astra at only one-tenth its price per token. At max effort, Terra is over three times as token efficient as Claude Opus 5.5, and one-fourth its price per token, resulting in a ~9x lower cost per task. Terra is also much quicker, completing tasksover three times fasterthan both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

OnMMMU-Pro, a benchmark of visual reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra outperforms GPT-5.6 Terra at every reasoning setting. It even nearly matches the scores of our most capable frontier model, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.1 Sol at much lower cost.

OSWorld 2.1tests how well AI agents use desktop apps to complete multistep tasks, such as building a 3D model from a technical drawing. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-5.6 Terra’s best score at a fraction of the cost per task.

This year, we’ve invested heavily in reducing hallucinations and factual errors produced by our models. On our internal benchmark of error-inducing prompts, the error rate at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% with GPT-5.6 Terra to 16.7% with GPT-6.1 Terra, a drop of nearly 37 percentage points. At maximum effort, the error rate fell by 18 percentage points to 4.3%, nearly matching the rates for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

GPT-6.1 Terra marks a substantial improvement over GPT-5.6 Terra for software engineering.Terminal-Bench 4.0tests how well coding agents solve problems from the command line, such as fixing a webpage whose layout shifts as it loads. At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6.1 Terra solves 50.3% of tasks, more than double GPT‑5.6 Terra’s published score of 21.5%. For the most complex coding tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the better choice.

Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1tests how well agents use code to carry out scientific research tasks, such as tracking cell divisions in a time-lapse video. At max reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-6.1 Sol at lower cost, coming within five points of Opus 5.5 at less than one-fifth the estimated cost.

As we make powerful AI more efficient and accessible, we continue training, testing, and refining our safeguards. GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra.

GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user’s task. More detail is available in thesystem card⁠(opens in a new window).

Starting today, GPT-6.1 Terra is available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API asgpt-6.1-terra.

Standard API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens.

articles.title: GPT-6.1 Sol
articles.content:
We’re introducingGPT-6.1 Sol, an upgrade to GPT-6 Sol that nearly matches GPT-6 Astra’s intelligence on agentic coding, computer use, and professional work at one-fifth of Astra’s standard input and output token prices. Cached input costs just$0.10 per million tokens—95% less than standard input pricing and 50% less than GPT-6 Sol’s cached input pricing—giving developers more room to build and run capable agents that reuse context across requests.

Our most intelligent model for the
best results.

Near-Astra intelligence for a fifth of the price.

Fast and efficient everyday work
at scale.

GPT-6.1 Sol offers a new balance of capability and cost for important everyday work. It delivers substantial improvements over GPT-6 Sol across complex professional tasks, from writing and debugging code to understanding documents and executing multi-step business workflows. On several of these evaluations, it approaches GPT-6 Astra’s performance at substantially lower cost.

OnDeepSWE v1.1, which evaluates complex software-engineering tasks in real codebases, GPT-6.1 Sol matches GPT-6 Astra at roughly one-fifth of the cost, while eclipsing GPT-6 Sol’s best score by 6.4 percentage points at a lower reasoning effort and cost.

InDeepSWE 1.1⁠⁠(opens in a new window), AI agents solve original, long-horizon software engineering tasks.

OnGDP.pdf, which measures how accurately models answer professional questions using complex PDF documents, including tables, charts, diagrams, and fine-print details, GPT-6.1 Sol scores higher than Opus 5.5 with fallbacks at less than half the cost per task across the tested reasoning settings. It also approaches GPT-6 Astra’s state-of-the-art performance at roughly one-fifth the cost per task.

InGDP.pdf⁠(opens in a new window), models must answer real-world prompts about complex PDFs pulled from professional workflows in finance, healthcare, legal, and seven other professional domains.

OnAutomationBench, which measures whether agents correctly complete multi-step business workflows, GPT-6.1 Sol scores 2.2 percentage points above Opus 5.5 at medium reasoning effort, at roughly a third of the cost. That score is also up 4.8 percentage points from GPT-6 Sol at the same setting.

InAutomationBench 1.0.6⁠⁠(opens in a new window), AI agents are tested on end-to-end workflows using 47 tools across sales, marketing, operations, support, finance, and HR. The datapoint for Claude Fable 5.1 understates its actual cost, as it omits the cost of fallbacks, which occurred on ~40% of tasks.

GPT-6.1 Sol also makes substantial progress on tasks that require interacting with computer applications. OnOSWorld 2.0’s offline set, which evaluates agents on demanding computer-use workflows, GPT-6.1 Sol outperforms GPT-6 Sol by seven percentage points at maximum reasoning effort at less than half the cost. It comes within 2.1 percentage points of Astra’s score at maximum reasoning effort at roughly one-seventh the cost per task.

InOSWorld 2.0⁠⁠(opens in a new window), AI agents attempt long-horizon computer-use workflows spanning everyday and professional tasks. We report the partial reward on the offline set from the v2026.08.08 release.

OnTerminal-Bench Science 0.1, which evaluates scientific workflows including data analysis, simulation, and theorem proving, GPT-6.1 Sol more than doubles GPT-6 Sol’s score at maximum reasoning effort at less than half the cost per task. At maximum effort, GPT-6.1 Sol costs $5.47 per task on average, compared with $23.21 for Opus 5.5 and $23.80 for Astra, delivering substantial scientific capability at over 75% lower cost than either model.

GPT-6 Astra still achieves the highest score among the models tested at 68.1%, and should be used for the most difficult scientific research tasks.

InTerminal-Bench Science 0.1⁠(opens in a new window), agents complete scientific research workflows using code and terminal tools, including analyzing data, running simulations, and fitting models.

GPT-6.1 Sol also improves factual accuracy on difficult prompts. Its largest factuality improvement over GPT-6 Sol comes at low reasoning effort, where it reduces the share of responses containing a factual error from 11.4% to 7.7%—a reduction of approximately 32%. Across the tested reasoning settings, its error rate remains within 1.9 percentage points of GPT-6 Astra’s, at less than one-fifth the cost per task.

This evaluation measures the share of answers containing at least one factual error on de-identified conversations where users flagged an earlier model’s error. These deliberately difficult prompts are not representative of typical usage.

We evaluate factuality on de-identified ChatGPT conversations where users had flagged a factual error from a prior model. These error-inducing conversations are not representative of typical usage, where factual errors are more rare.

GPT-6.1 Sol shows substantial improvements over GPT-6 Sol in our alignment evaluations, bringing it closer to GPT-6 Astra.

GPT-6.1 Sol is more transparent about its limitations and more reliable at respecting user intent and safety constraints. In challenging evaluations, it shows lower failure rates than GPT-6 Sol on transparency about broken search tools, respecting explicit restrictions, and avoiding unauthorized outcomes during agentic tasks. We observed no attempts to bypass an automated safety reviewer, matching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Sol. Full details can be found in theGPT-6.1 Sol system card addendum⁠(opens in a new window).

The evaluations below deliberately test challenging situations and do not measure failure rates in typical use.

GPT-6.1 Sol is available starting today to all Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. GPT-6.1 Sol is not yet available in Chat. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API as gpt-6.1-sol. Its standard API prices are $2 per million input tokens, $0.10 per million cached input tokens, and $10 per million output tokens. In the coming days, we’ll also offer GPT-6.1 SolUltrafast⁠, with up to 8x faster token generation compared to its standard speed in Codex.

Evaluations of GPT were performed in our research environment or via our API, which may provide slightly different output from production ChatGPT due to differences in the system prompts, tools available, efforts, etc. Evaluations of competitor models were taken from publicly available reports.

articles.title: Research
articles.content:
October 26, 2026

We are announcing three newdiscoveriesin mathematics, computer science, and physics about harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory.

Our release process continues to evolve in response to feedback from theassociatedacademic communities. In our view, these manuscripts are best understood as a form of raw research data. To convert this raw research data into scientific understanding, in this release we are experimenting with a new approach. We reached out to external experts and asked them to act as shepherds, organizing groups to understand the new results. They advised three different release strategies:

For the math result, release the AI output, leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.

For the computer science result, form an external group of collaborators to explain the result, while making the AI output publicly available for anyone to examine and build on.

For the physics result, form an external group of collaborators and defer to them on the release of materials.

We do not yet know which of these three approaches will be most useful, and we welcome feedback on what works and what we can improve.

The external collaborations will follow four principles:

Transparency.We are transparent about the existence of our collaborations. Participants will not be asked to sign nondisclosure agreements and will be free to discuss the work, share intermediate products, and publish their conclusions.

No Academic Credit.We do not seek academic credit for the discoveries produced by our internal models. Inviting a researcher to help steward a collaboration also does not imply that they or their working group made the original discovery.

Recognition.This group should receive recognition for the understanding they develop, the writeups they author, and the other materials they create. The group will also help ensure that the work appropriately credits researchers, techniques, and ideas that it draws on.

Independence.Participation is voluntary and unpaid. Working-group members participate independently, and their conclusions are their own. They do not speak on behalf of OpenAI, and OpenAI does not speak on their behalf.

We will turn over materials and artifacts related to these results to the collaborations. For the computer science collaboration, the group has decided to make the natural language proof and Lean formalization public immediately, and we are publishing them directly to our GitHub repository. For the physics collaboration, the group has decided to hold off on releasing the AI-produced artifacts and instead work on writing it up themselves.

All of these approaches involve tradeoffs. On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community. On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.

The result in mathematics concerns harmonic analysis. In 1991, Sogge proposed the local smoothing conjecture, which concerns the behavior of waves as they become focused. In particular, the conjecture states that the most extreme focusing must be short-lived. The amount of focusing at a typical random time is always much smaller than what can happen at the worst-case time. This is a familiar pattern throughout mathematics: what can happen in the worst case is more extreme than what is observed after averaging. Because of how fundamental this conjectured phenomenon is, it also has wide ranging implications throughout mathematical analysis. For instance, it implies the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture.

In 2019,Guth, Wang, and Zhang⁠(opens in a new window)proved the local smoothing conjecture in two spatial dimensions. In 2025,Wang and Zahl⁠(opens in a new window)proved the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions. Our models produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions. The new proof is based on a novel auxiliary partial differential equation.

We obtained our AI output on October 18th, 2026, which was formalized in Lean the following day, and then we reached out to an expert to discuss forming a collaboration around this result. Following their recommendation, we decided to release the AI output publicly, following the same strategy for this result as our October 6th, 2026release⁠. We have released both anAI natural language output writeup⁠(opens in a new window)produced by our models and aLean proof⁠(opens in a new window)in our public GitHub repository.

The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture about the computational complexity of Boolean formula satisfiability, a problem deeply related to the P vs. NP problem. The ETH has been widely believed to be true, and has been used in hundreds of papers to derive conditional computational hardness results across a wide variety of fields including graph theory, computational biology, databases, computational geometry, and more. Surprisingly, our system has recently proved that the ETH is false, a result that was subsequently verified in Lean. The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become, and may help guide the search for better algorithms. Finding such algorithms, and turning theoretical advances into practical improvements, will require significant further research.

This work will be verified and shepherded by a group led by Russell Impagliazzo (UC San Diego), Ramamohan Paturi (UC San Diego), and Ryan Williams (MIT). All three are experts in algorithm design and complexity theory.

Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with Francis Zane, are the original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and have authored a⁠(opens in a new window)number⁠(opens in a new window)of⁠(opens in a new window)influential⁠(opens in a new window)⁠(opens in a new window)papers⁠(opens in a new window)on thetopic⁠(opens in a new window)over the last 30 years.

Williams has refuted⁠(opens in a new window)strong⁠(opens in a new window)⁠(opens in a new window)versions⁠(opens in a new window)of the ETH, used ETH for⁠(opens in a new window)hardness⁠(opens in a new window)⁠(opens in a new window)results⁠(opens in a new window), and connected⁠(opens in a new window)algorithms⁠(opens in a new window)and⁠(opens in a new window)lower bounds⁠(opens in a new window).

We have agreed to the group’s requests that all raw data of the results be made public to facilitate independent verification by the community, and that OpenAI commit to funding a conference to understand the implications of this work on the field as a whole. The group invites the community to help organize an open examination of the ETH claim and to discuss the broader questions that AI-generated breakthroughs raise about verification, access, credit, and the future of research.

Our AI found its natural language disproof for the ETH on October 16th, 2026 and then subsequently we formalized the result in Lean on October 17th, 2026, which led us to develop the collaboration described here. To that end, we have released both anAI natural language output writeup⁠(opens in a new window)produced by our models and aLean proof⁠(opens in a new window)in our public GitHub repository.

Computational complexity has many open questions and conjectures, whose proofs or refutations have so far eluded the best efforts of scientists. We hope that humans with AI can provide new understanding in this field, and shed light on the inherent capabilities and limits of efficient computation.

The physics collaboration will understand and explain a result that gives a mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics. Our work builds onBalaban’s approach⁠(opens in a new window)inconstructive quantum field theory. As a subproblem, this work also includes a proof of the existence of pure Yang–Mills theory, which is part of theQuantum Yang–Mills Theory Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize problem⁠(opens in a new window).

The Standard Model describes the interaction of fundamental subatomic particles for three of the four fundamental forces, excepting gravity. The existence proof pertains to the simplest grand unified theory that includes the gauge fields and fermions of the Standard Model (as the Standard Model itself cannot be extrapolated to arbitrarily short distances). QCD describes the interaction of particles such as quarks and gluons via the strong force. Pure Yang–Mills theory only describes the self-interactions of the gluons, the force carriers, rather than matter such as quarks.

David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov that will shepherd this work.

Gross’s 1973 work on asymptotic freedom in Yang-Mills theories helped establish QCD as the theory of the strong interactions and earned him a share of the2004 Nobel Prize in Physics⁠(opens in a new window). Asymptotic freedom is also the key mechanism underlying the existence of these theories as mathematically rigorous objects.

Jaffe formulated theQuantum Yang-Mills Theory Millenium Prize problem⁠(opens in a new window)with Witten and also envisioned the idea of Millennium Prize problems and co-founded the Clay Mathematics Institute.

Douglas has already been a steward of this problem over the last 20 years,reporting on its status in 2004⁠(opens in a new window)and then providing acomprehensive update on the progress⁠(opens in a n...
articles.summary: OpenAI가 조화해석, 계산복잡도 이론, 양자장론에 관한 세 가지 새로운 발견을 발표했다. 다만 AI가 만든 원고를 완성된 과학적 이해보다는 원시 연구 데이터로 규정하고, 분야별로 외부 연구자가 결과를 이해하고 설명하는 서로 다른 공개 방식을 시험한다고 밝혔다. 수학은 AI 출력을 공개하고, 컴퓨터과학은 외부 협업팀의 해설과 공개를 병행하며, 물리학은 협업팀에 자료 공개 판단을 맡긴다. 제공된 자료만으로 개별 발견의 내용이나 검증 수준을 판단할 수는 없으며, AI 연구 결과의 검토와 공로 배분 절차가 핵심 쟁점이다.

articles.title: Security
articles.content:
October 26, 2026

As AI accelerates software development, engineering and application-security teams need ways to investigate code changes and address vulnerabilities while keeping people in control. CodeRabbit is usingGPT‑6.1 Solas the primary model in its security agent to extend review beyond individual changes and help developers understand risks across complex codebases.

A pull request can affect shared libraries, dependencies and safeguards elsewhere in an application. GPT‑6.1 Sol helps CodeRabbit connect behavior across files and components to surface potential security issues. CodeRabbit’s review is independent of the agent that wrote the code and complements established scanners. Its system also uses other frontier models and security tooling.

During pull-request review, Sol helps analyze changes as developers work. In Deep Scan, it supports broader investigation across repositories, including dependencies and how components interact. CodeRabbit Secure extends that investigation to linked repositories, such as a shared authentication library, to help teams understand how a weakness could affect the wider system.

CodeRabbit reports using GPT‑6.1 Sol to flag security-related issues across thousands of repositories and organizations. These findings feed into the pull-request workflows developers already use to review and improve their code.

CodeRabbit Secure connects investigation to remediation. For user-selected findings, it can attempt exploit verification in an isolated sandbox without testing production systems. For supported issues, it can draft a pull request with a proposed fix for a person to review and approve.

This work shows how frontier reasoning can support software security: understanding risks beyond an individual change, helping validate findings and turning them into proposed fixes. Human reviewers remain responsible for deciding which changes to ship.

articles.title: What's new in the hf CLI and huggingface_hub library
articles.content:
We've been shipping a lot of features inhuggingface_hub/hfCLI these past few weeks across Hugging Face Jobs, Storage Buckets, Sandboxes, cache optimization, DX improvements for downloading and uploading and more. Here is a recap of the highlights.

The same file often lives in many repos. For example, FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.1-schnell and FLUX.1-Krea-dev all ship the same 9.5 GB text encoder. Your cache now stores each Xet file once, and other repos that need it get a link instead of a new download: no bytes transferred, no extra disk used. There is nothing to configure.

Cleaning up got easier too. You can remove a single cached file, like one GGUF quantization, without deleting the whole repo, andhf cache pruneremoves shared files that no repo uses anymore:

Jobs got many small upgrades that add up:

Every Job now gets a name automatically, from its image or script and a short hash of the command, so reruns of the same command are easy to find.

A UV script can also carry its own Job config, in a[tool.hf-jobs]table of its header.hf jobs uv runpicks it up, so the script always runs on the right image and hardware. Flags you pass on the command line still win.

A webhook can also start a Job instead of calling a URL. Each time a repo or a Storage Bucket you watch changes, the Job runs again, with the event in theWEBHOOK_PAYLOADenvironment variable. Webhooks can now watch Storage Buckets, and pass secrets like yourHF_TOKENto the Job, so it can read and write on the Hub:

<job_id>is a Job you ran before: each event starts a new Job with the same setup.--secrets HF_TOKENpasses the token you are logged in with.

Jobs commands also behave better in scripts and agents:hf jobs statsprints a snapshot and exits (add-fto follow),hf jobs logswithout-fno longer hangs, andhf jobs runreconnects when the log stream drops. In your terminal, it also shows why a Job is still waiting for hardware.

Downloading data from a Storage Bucket is much faster:HfFileSystemnow downloads Xet files withhf_xet, straight to disk. In our benchmark on HF Jobs, downloading a 2.15 GB parquet file went from 2 minutes to about 7 seconds.

Thedatasetslibrary readshf://paths throughHfFileSystem, soload_datasetgets the same speedup starting withdatasets5.1.0, the first release that works withhuggingface_hub2.x. Loading the same file went from 130 seconds to about 17.

HfFileSystemcaches listings, so files added to a Storage Bucket by another process used to stay invisible until you cleared the cache. Withlive_follow=True, listings update as new files land.

You can also set a Storage Bucket's visibility when you create it, or change it later withhf buckets settings my-org/my-bucket --public.

Sandboxes (experimental) are isolated machines that you start from Python or the CLI, run commands in, and move files in and out of. They run on Jobs, so any Docker image works, on CPU or GPU. This is useful when an agent needs to run code it just wrote, away from your laptop.

Recent releases added custom labels, to find the sandboxes a run created or track costs, and a round of security hardening.

📚Sandboxes guide

AI agents are now a big part of who uses thehfCLI. On a given day, 1 in 3 users of thehfCLI is an AI agent. For uploads, more than half of the users who upload to the Hub with thehfCLI do it through an AI agent.

Thehf-cliskillmakes them faster, not more accurate. Recent models already know a lot about thehfCLI and find their way withhf --help, so they solve Hub tasks just as well without the skill. With it, they skip the trial and error. We ran DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Kimi-K3 through Hugging Face Inference Providers on 28 Hub tasks, with and without the skill.

Both models solved 99 to 100% of the tasks either way, but with the skill they needed about a third fewer turns and almost stopped calling--help.

Downloads and uploads got smoother:

You can also check how much ZeroGPU time you have left, from the CLI or in Python. Apps and agents built on ZeroGPU Spaces can use it to warn users before they hit the daily limit.

Ask your agent to upgrade thehfCLI to the latest version or runhf updateyourself. All the details are in therelease notes.
articles.summary: Hugging Face가 hf CLI와 huggingface_hub의 캐시, Jobs, Storage Buckets 관련 개선 사항을 공개했다. 여러 저장소에서 사용하는 동일한 Xet 파일을 한 번만 저장하고 링크로 재사용해 중복 다운로드와 디스크 사용을 줄이며, 개별 캐시 파일 삭제와 미사용 공유 파일 정리도 지원한다. Jobs에는 스크립트 내 실행 설정, 저장소·버킷 변경에 따른 웹훅 실행, 로그 연결 복구 등이 추가됐다. 모델 자산 관리와 이벤트 기반 작업 자동화를 개선하는 실무형 업데이트다.

articles.title: Research
articles.content:
October 26, 2026

OpenAI Economic Research releases data for researchers to explore questions on AI and labor more deeply.

Today, we are releasingOpenAI Signals data that explores165 work activities across nearly 100 countries, revealing how consumers use ChatGPT for work. This data gives researchers a new way to study AI’s role in the economy, with new information on the work activities people bring to ChatGPT—from preparing instructional materials and developing marketing content to programming and analyzing business data.

Researchers can use this data to explore how ChatGPT use for work differs across countries, track changes over time, and match this data to other economic indicators. The release connects ChatGPT usage to 165 work activity categories called Intermediate Work Activities (IWAs). IWAs are commonly-used categories of tasks for the kinds of work people do across occupations. The data is represented quarterly, spanning a period from the first quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026.

Our new data draws on O*NET, a standardized framework that groups occupation-specific tasks into broader categories of work activities shared across occupations. Using a common framework helps researchers compare ChatGPT use with other types of occupational and employment data.

The interactive chart below can be used to explore these work activities within a specific country over time, moving from broad activity groups to more specific activities. The data shows wide variation across countries in how people use ChatGPT for work.

Explore the work people bring to ChatGPT. Select an activity group to see the tasks within it, see how those change over time, or choose a country to explore its mix of work-related messages.

Connecting this data to IWAs revealed that work-related use became less concentrated in the most common activities. That means that countries tended to specialize in their work over time, and different countries specialized in different types of work. These differences might reflect variation in the kind of work done across countries or varying access to AI tools. Exploring these questions is one example of many that researchers can pursue with this new data.

Across 74 countries observed in every quarter, the ten most common activities represented an average of 51.1% of each country’s classified work messages in Q3 2026, down from 56.0% in Q1 2025.

Connecting ChatGPT usage data with IWAs lets researchers compare ChatGPT messages with activities performed across U.S. jobs. The paired visualizations below compare how people use ChatGPT with the activities performed across U.S. jobs. This comparison shows the difference in how people use ChatGPT for work and the actual work being done in the U.S. economy. The two distributions differ substantially, largely because about 43% of the employment-weighted task mix for mapped U.S. occupations falls into Other IWAs, outside the individually reported categories. These include activities such as moving materials, operating vehicles, and maintaining health or medical records. These omitted categories did not meet our threshold for consistent representation in the original U.S. ChatGPT sample.

Select an activity to see how much it appears in ChatGPT usage versus the overall U.S. economy.

This release builds on OpenAI Signals, our ongoing effort to share evidence about how people use AI. The data covers work-related messages on individual ChatGPT plans and does not include enterprise messages or Codex use. We invite researchers to explore the data, connect it with other sources, and investigate what these patterns mean for workers and businesses.

To protect users’ privacy, researchers do not read individual conversations. Automated systems classify messages after identifying information is removed. We publish aggregated statistics, withhold results for small groups, and add statistical noise to protect individual messages.

articles.summary: OpenAI가 약 100개국의 ChatGPT 업무 활용을 165개 업무 활동으로 분류한 Signals 데이터를 공개했다. 데이터는 2025년 1분기부터 2026년 3분기까지 분기별로 제공되며, O*NET의 표준 업무 분류를 사용해 다른 직업·고용 지표와 비교할 수 있도록 했다. 국가별 활용 구성과 시간에 따른 변화를 연구하는 데 유용하지만, 소비자의 ChatGPT 사용 데이터이므로 이를 전체 노동시장이나 생산성 효과의 직접 측정치로 해석해서는 안 된다.

articles.title: Nested Sparsity for Scalable Pretraining and Continual Learning
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.31818v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers, the standard backbone for modern large-scale deep learning, employ conditional computation: only a sparse subset of model weights is used in each forward pass. In MoE transformers, this sparsity arises in the MoE operator, which generalizes the multi-layer perceptron in the classical transformer. In this work, we explore an alternative mechanism for conditional computation that analogously generalizes the attention operator. The sparsity induced by this mechanism naturally nests (i.e., hierarchically composes) with the sparsity induced by the MoE operator. We show that a transformer employing this nested sparsity mechanism, which we call Nestor, performs better than a conventional MoE transformer at equal compute and equal sparsity in language model pretraining. We also show that Nestor is well-suited for continual pretraining: it can be adapted to longer contexts more effectively than conventional MoEs, as well as adapt more efficiently to new domains while forgetting less on old domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length grow. Our results demonstrate the potential of alternative conditional computation mechanisms for deep neural network architectures. Code and checkpoints are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ma-Lab-Berkeley/Nestor .
articles.summary: Nestor 연구는 어텐션 연산의 조건부 계산을 기존 전문가 혼합 모델의 희소성과 계층적으로 결합하는 구조를 제안했다. 연구진은 동일한 계산량과 희소성 조건에서 기존 MoE보다 언어모델 사전학습 성능이 높고, 긴 문맥 적응과 새 도메인 학습에서도 효율 및 기존 지식 보존이 개선됐다고 보고했다. 모델·데이터·문맥 규모를 늘려도 이점이 유지됐으며 코드와 체크포인트를 공개했다. 조건부 계산을 전문가 계층 이외로 확장하는 설계 방향을 제시하지만, 초록에는 구체적인 성능 차이가 제시되지 않았다.

articles.title: HyScale: Scaling Long-Context Training for Learned Sparse Attention
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.32057v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present HyScale, a long-context training system for learned sparse attention. Learned sparse attention is a promising architecture for million-token contexts, widely adopted in production since DeepSeek-V3.2. Selection, however, grows into the training bottleneck. For each query, it scores every previous token whereas sparse attention reads only $k$; worse, current systems materialize a full score table and repeat selection during recomputation. Our key insight is that the output of selection is not an activation, but rather a set of indices. Building on it, HyScale introduces HyTopK and selection replay. HyTopK finds each query's exact top-$k$ on the fly without a score table, while selection replay reuses forward-pass selection in recomputation. Together with holistic system optimizations tackling end-to-end training challenges, HyScale speeds up GLM-5.1 training on 1M-token sequences by 2.07$\times$ over Megatron-LM on 512 H20 GPUs. It also speeds up the CSA layers of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and the QSA layers of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by 2.01$\times$ and 1.57$\times$ at 1M tokens on 32 H800 GPUs.
articles.summary: HyScale은 학습형 희소 어텐션의 긴 문맥 학습에서 토큰 선택 과정이 병목이 되는 문제를 다룬다. 전체 점수표를 만들지 않고 정확한 상위 k개 인덱스를 구하는 HyTopK와, 재계산 시 순전파의 선택 결과를 재사용하는 기법을 결합했다. 연구진은 H20 GPU 512개를 사용한 100만 토큰 GLM-5.1 학습에서 Megatron-LM 대비 2.07배 속도 향상을 보고했다. 희소 어텐션 자체뿐 아니라 선택과 재계산 비용까지 최적화해야 실제 장문 학습 효율을 높일 수 있음을 보여준다.

articles.title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.31846v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.
articles.summary: Self-Direction은 에이전트가 실패에서 얻은 교훈을 경량 저랭크 어댑터에 즉시 학습하고, 이후 유사한 문제에서 재사용하는 방법이다. 기본 모델 가중치는 고정하며, 어댑터 하나당 추가 학습 파라미터는 기본 모델의 약 0.02%에 해당한다. Qwen 계열 에이전트의 GAIA, Claw-Eval, Terminal-Bench 2.1 평가에서 전체 성공률이 8.9~17.0%포인트 상승했다고 연구진은 보고했다. 세션을 넘어 오류 교정을 유지하는 접근으로, 일부 어댑터는 추가 학습 없이 여러 새 과제로 전이됐지만 일반화 범위는 평가된 과제에 한정된다.

articles.title: BARC-Bench: Benign Asks, Risky Consequences
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.32024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Task instructions from users for agents are inherently underspecified, especially regarding safety boundaries--creating behavioral risks. To study these risks, we introduce BARC-Bench, a collection of 110 tasks across nine simulated workspace environments where benign requests leave openings for unsafe actions. In this benchmark, we evaluate agent behavior against safety boundaries established by workspace records, implicit environmental context, and unstated social norms. For example, an agent asked to schedule off-boarding discussions must arrange the meeting without prematurely revealing an employee's resignation through a shared calendar invitation. Evaluating four frontier model configurations across five attempts per task reveals that models are not consistently safe: the share of tasks completed safely on all five attempts ranges from 9.1% to 72.7%, with even the strongest configuration producing a safety violation on 27.3% of tasks. These results highlight an asymmetric operational risk: while models frequently complete complex workflows, their inability to consistently respect unstated boundaries presents a substantial barrier to safe autonomous delegation.
articles.summary: BARC-Bench는 선의의 업무 요청에도 명시되지 않은 안전 경계가 존재한다는 점을 평가하는 벤치마크다. 9개 모의 업무 환경의 110개 과제를 통해 공유 일정에서 퇴사 정보를 성급히 노출하는 상황처럼 환경 기록과 사회적 맥락을 고려해야 하는 행동을 시험한다. 네 가지 프런티어 모델 구성에서 과제별 다섯 번의 시도를 모두 안전하게 완료한 비율은 9.1~72.7%였으며, 가장 좋은 구성도 과제의 27.3%에서 한 번 이상 안전 위반을 일으켰다. 업무 완료율만으로는 자율 위임의 안전성을 평가하기 어렵다는 결과다.

articles.title: TACS-RF: Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave Modules
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.31882v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present the framework of TACS-RF - a Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave modules. In this framework, a large-language-model (LLM) coding agent (Claude Opus 4.8) directly drives industry-standard electronic-design-automation (EDA) tools such as Cadence Virtuoso/Spectre, Calibre, Cadence EMX, and Ansys HFSS to design RF and mmWave modules. We validate the framework through the agentic design of a 240-251 GHz sub-THz transmitter in a 90 nm SiGe BiCMOS process. The agent semi-autonomously designed the sub-blocks including a 60 GHz push-push Colpitts VCO with second-harmonic extraction, multistage differential cascode power drivers, a push-push frequency doubler, a differential bowtie antenna, and all the interstage matching networks. The transmitter chain with parasitic-extracted devices and EM-verified passives delivers +5.1 to +6.3 dBm across an 11 GHz varactor-only tuning range, phase noise of -80 to -88 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset while consuming a DC power of 361 mW. We describe the agent-driven design flow and the resulting division of labor between human and agent, taking a step toward a "text-to-ASIC" future for designing RF/mmWave hardware.
articles.summary: TACS-RF는 LLM 코딩 에이전트가 Cadence Virtuoso·Spectre, Calibre, EMX, Ansys HFSS 등 산업용 EDA 도구를 직접 구동해 RF·밀리미터파 회로를 설계하는 프레임워크다. 연구진은 90nm SiGe BiCMOS 공정의 240~251GHz 송신기 설계를 통해 발진기, 전력 구동단, 주파수 배가기, 안테나 등의 반자율 설계 흐름을 제시했다. 기생성분 추출과 전자기 검증을 반영한 송신기 체인에서 361mW 소비전력과 +5.1~+6.3dBm 출력을 보고했다. 전문 하드웨어 설계로 에이전트 활용 범위를 넓힌 사례지만, 제공 자료에는 제작 칩의 실측 검증이 명시되지 않았다.

articles.title: “딥페이크로 얼굴 도용하면 AI가 잡아낸다”…딥브레인AI, 인물 식별·차단 기술 개발
articles.content:
생성형 인공지능(AI)으로 타인의 얼굴을 무단 도용하거나 특정 인물을 사칭하는 딥페이크 콘텐츠를 사전에 차단할 수 있는 인물 식별 기술이 개발됐다. 보호 대상 인물의 얼굴을 데이터베이스(DB)와 비교해 도용 가능성을 판별하고, 위험 수준에 따라 콘텐츠 생성 요청을 자동 차단하거나 담당자가 추가 검토하도록 지원하는 방식이다.

생성형 AI 전문기업 딥브레인AI(DeepBrain AI, 대표 장세영)는 이미지와 영상 속 인물을 분석해 초상권 침해와 인물 사칭 위험에 대응하는 ‘페이스 아이디(Face ID) 판별’ 기술 개발을 완료했다고 27일 밝혔다.

이번 기술은 딥브레인AI의 생성형 AI 안전 엔진 ‘AI 가드(AI Guard)’에 적용되는 인물 식별 기능으로, 사전에 등록된 보호 대상 인물과 콘텐츠 속 얼굴의 동일 인물 여부를 판단하는 데 초점을 맞췄다. 이 플랫폼은 얼굴의 외형이 달라지더라도 보호 대상 인물을 식별하면서, 서로 닮은 다른 사람을 동일 인물로 잘못 판단하는 오인식 가능성을 줄이는 것이다.

이를 위해 안경과 모자 착용 여부, 앞머리와 수염, 얼굴 각도, 표정 등 인식 결과에 영향을 미치는 다양한 조건을 고려해 판정 기준을 차등 적용하도록 설계했다.

얼굴 분석 과정에서는 이미지에서 검출한 얼굴을 주요 특징점에 맞춰 정렬한 뒤, 얼굴의 특징을 수치화한 ‘512차원 특징 벡터(512-dimensional Feature Vector)’로 변환한다. 이후 등록된 보호 대상 인물의 특징 데이터와 비교하고, 유사도 결과를 추가로 재정렬해 판별 정확도를 높이는 방식이다.

딥브레인AI에 따르면 특정 인물 인식 성능은 국제공인시험기관의 시험에서 과제 기준을 충족했다. 구체적인 정확도와 오인식률 수치는 이번 발표에서 공개하지 않았다.

실제 서비스에서는 판별 결과를 ‘안전·주의·일치’의 3단계로 구분해 활용할 수 있다. 보호 대상 인물과 일치하는 것으로 판정된 콘텐츠 생성 요청은 자동으로 차단하고, 추가 확인이 필요한 주의 단계의 요청은 담당자가 검토하도록 설정할 수 있다. 안전 단계는 별도의 위험 신호가 확인되지 않은 요청을 구분하는 데 활용된다.

특히 성능 평가 환경과 실제 운영 서버에 동일한 판정 기준값을 적용해 시험 과정에서 확인한 결과가 서비스 환경에서도 일관되게 유지되도록 했다.

영상 콘텐츠에 대한 분석 기능도 갖췄다. 일정한 간격으로 영상 프레임을 추출해 얼굴을 식별하고, 동일 인물이 등장하는 시점을 연결해 구간별 판별 결과를 제공한다. 담당자는 영상 전체의 판정 결과뿐 아니라 최고 유사도, 일치·주의 판정 건수, 인물별 등장 구간 등을 확인할 수 있다. 이를 통해 긴 영상을 처음부터 끝까지 직접 살펴보지 않고도 추가 검토가 필요한 장면을 선별할 수 있다.

보호 대상 인물의 데이터베이스를 구축하고 갱신하는 과정도 자동화했다. 인물 목록을 입력하면 여러 검색 소스에서 관련 이미지를 수집하고, 신원 확인과 품질 검사를 거쳐 등록에 적합한 이미지를 선별한다. 흐릿한 사진이나 동명이인의 이미지, 단체사진, 중복 사진 등은 제외하도록 구성했다.

신규 인물을 추가할 때는 해당 인물의 특징 벡터만 계산하고, 서비스 중단 없이 검색 인덱스를 교체할 수 있도록 설계해 데이터베이스 관리 부담도 줄였다. 딥브레인AI는 얼굴 데이터베이스 구축·관리용 4종과 인물 판별용 2종 등 총 6종의 응용프로그램 인터페이스(API)를 제공한다.

이를 통해 콘텐츠 제작·공유 플랫폼과 공공기관 등이 기존 서비스에 인물 식별 및 도용 방지 기능을 연동할 수 있도록 지원할 계획이다.

이번 기술은 딥페이크 영상 자체의 진위를 판별하는 방식과는 구별된다. 생성형 AI로 제작됐는지 여부를 직접 확인하기보다, 콘텐츠에 등장하거나 생성에 사용되는 얼굴이 사전에 보호 대상으로 등록된 인물과 일치하는지를 확인하는 데 목적이 있다.

따라서 보호 대상 인물이 등록되지 않았거나 얼굴을 식별하기 어려운 콘텐츠에서는 적용 범위가 제한될 수 있다. 또한 동일 인물로 판정됐다는 사실만으로 초상권 침해나 불법 도용 여부가 확정되는 것은 아니므로, 실제 서비스에서는 이용 목적과 권한 등에 대한 추가 확인이 필요하다.

장세영 딥브레인AI 대표는 “얼굴 인식 기술에서 중요한 것은 보호 대상 인물을 정확하게 찾아내는 동시에 다른 사람을 동일 인물로 잘못 판단하는 오인식을 최소화하는 것”이라며 “다양한 촬영 환경과 얼굴 변화 조건에서도 신뢰할 수 있는 판별 기술을 바탕으로 인물 도용 방지와 초상권 보호 역량을 강화하고, 안전한 생성형 AI 콘텐츠 활용 환경을 조성해 나가겠다”고 밝혔다.

생성형 AI를 이용한 인물 합성과 영상 제작이 쉬워지면서 콘텐츠 플랫폼의 사전 식별 및 관리 기술도 중요해지고 있다. 이번 페이스 아이디 판별 기술은 보호 대상 인물의 식별부터 콘텐츠 생성 요청 차단, 영상 검토, 데이터베이스 관리까지 연결해 초상권 보호 업무를 자동화하는 데 초점을 맞춘 것으로 평가된다.
articles.summary: 딥브레인AI가 보호 대상 인물의 얼굴과 콘텐츠 속 얼굴을 비교해 생성 요청을 차단하거나 추가 검토로 보내는 ‘페이스 아이디 판별’ 기술을 개발했다. 얼굴을 정렬한 뒤 512차원 특징 벡터로 변환해 등록 데이터와 비교하며, 영상 구간별 식별과 데이터베이스 관리·판별용 6종 API도 제공한다. 이는 딥페이크의 진위를 직접 판정하는 기술이 아니라 등록 인물과의 동일성을 확인하는 방식으로, 미등록 인물이나 식별이 어려운 얼굴에는 적용 범위가 제한된다. 회사는 공인시험에서 과제 기준을 충족했다고 밝혔으나 정확도와 오인식률은 공개하지 않았으며, 동일 인물 판정만으로 불법 도용이 확정되는 것도 아니다.

articles.title: Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang
articles.content: Tsinghua University and CUHK researchers open-sourced AKV, a serving system for KV cache engineering in LLM agents. Instead of summarizing old history, agents drop selected KV cache entries and keep reusing the rest. Across 3 models and 4 agent benchmarks, average cost falls 27.7%. Average task score rises 1.7 points. The code is Apache-2.0 licensed and builds on SGLang. TL;DR What it is: Serving system plus policy library, no weights. Tested on GPT-OSS-120B (5.1B active), MiniMax-M2.7 (230B total, 10B active) and MiroThinker-1.7-Mini (30B total, 3B active). Runs on: NVIDIA GPUs via SGLang. Paper used 8 A800-80GB GPUs in BF16. Quick start serves GPT-OSS-120B on 2 GPUs (tensor parallel 2). Performance: 27.7% lower average cost and +1.7 points average score versus threshold summarization. Best: GPT-OSS-120B on SWE-bench Verified: cost per task 20.0 to 9.7 cents, score 40.0 to 43.2. Worst: MiniMax-M2.7 on BrowseComp-Plus scores 58.9, 3.4 points below Text Engineering’s 62.3. What is cache engineering, and how is it different from context engineering? AKV is a Tsinghua serving system that lets LLM agents drop and reposition their own KV cache. Context engineering trims or summarizes the text history. Editing that prefix invalidates every later KV state. The retained suffix must then be re-prefilled. Harnesses therefore summarize late and aggressively, which can lose details from middle rounds. Cache engineering leaves the text trajectory untouched. It only changes which KV entries stay visible to attention. Retained entries are reused without recomputation. They can still carry information from dropped messages. In the research paper’s cost analysis, KV cache reads made up 82.4% of total API cost. How does AKV work? AKV defines 3 cache operations. Append is the standard update for new tokens. Drop removes selected entries from future attention without changing positions. Repos rewrites retained keys to positions 0 through r-1 using a RoPE rotation. Values stay unchanged, so no hidden states are recomputed. In ablations, adding Repos raised GPT-OSS-120B’s BrowseComp-Plus pass rate from 55% to 62%. The hard part is serving. Identical tokens can produce different cache states under different operation histories. Plain prefix matching could reuse the wrong states. AKV extends SGLang’s radix tree with drop and reposition nodes. It frees dropped KV only when no active request still needs it. Segment-batch attention restores evicted states in 1 prefill pass. What does the AKV API look like? The interface is stateless and OpenAI-compatible. Clients send the full message history and two optional fields. drop_message maps a trigger message index to the messages to drop. reposition lists the indices after which positions get compacted. A CachePolicy builds those fields from a trigger, a selector and a reposition rule. Built-in policies are turn-based, token-based or model-based. A CacheTool lets the model call drop_context itself. How does AKV perform on agent benchmarks? The main policy is a tool-response rolling drop that keeps the latest 12 tool responses. The Standard baseline summarizes at 96K tokens (192K for MiroThinker). Text Engineering summarizes at 48K. Benchmarks are BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA-Text, SWE-bench Verified and xbench-DeepSearch-2510. articles.title: Nace AI Releases Drex for Search for AI Agents: 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus With 12.6 Search Calls
articles.content: Nace AI has released Drex for Search, which brings its Drex decision models to document search. Drex for Search is a retrieval layer that helps people and agents find evidence. Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode call it through CLI, SDKs, MCP or REST. In Nace’s evaluation, it scores 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus with GPT-5, using 12.6 search calls per question. TL;DR Size: a hosted search system built to search over 1M+ files. It pairs with an answering model such as GPT-5, Gemini 3.5 Flash or Qwen 27B. Runs on: Nace’s managed cloud, a dedicated cloud, your own AWS or Azure account, or on-prem and air-gapped. Performance: ranked #1 or #2 on 3 of 4 public leaderboards, per Nace. Best: 77.5% R@1 on VisDocAgentBench, 10 points above Claude Opus 5 (67.5%). What did Nace AI release? Nace AI frames search as a series of decisions. Drex for Search applies its Drex models to those decisions. Drex scores given options with a calibrated probability each, in 1 forward pass. That makes it cheap enough for every agent step. The release targets classic RAG, which Nace sums up as chunk, embed, top-k, hope. The pipeline breaks in 3 cases: the answer sits in a table on page 23 the answer needs 2 hops across files the answer is inside a scanned PDF How does Drex for Search work inside an agent? Nace describes 3 steps: Classify: Before any search runs, Drex decides if the question needs a quick lookup or an agent. The agent route reads documents and queries tables. Squeeze: Drex walks the workspace level by level: folder, file, section, page. Inside a sheet, it narrows to table and column. Each level keeps only what can hold the answer. Answer: Only the kept pages and tables reach the LLM. The answer cites the file and page. Depth is fixed, so Nace says a million files take as many steps as a thousand. How much does it help coding agents? Nace AI tested 9 agent and model pairs on OfficeQA Pro, a 133-question benchmark over U.S. Treasury Bulletins. Key highlights: 6% more answers right, 62% fewer steps, 56% fewer tokens, and 2.3x faster. Files: PDFs and scans, xlsx, csv and Parquet, mp3 and mp4, docx, pptx, md, json and txt. Citations: every answer names the file and the page, row or minute it came from. Workspaces: isolated, with their own index and knowledge graph, and shareable with invited members. Storage: upload files or folders, or keep workspaces in your own S3 bucket or Azure Blob container. Zero retention: available with your own storage. Domains: Tax, M&A, SEC 10-K, Contracts, or your own. How does it perform on BrowseComp-Plus? BrowseComp-Plus asks a deep-research agent 830 multi-hop questions over about 100K fixed web documents. With GPT-5, Nace AI reports: 92.05% accuracy, #2 of 86 entries on the leaderboard. 12.61 search calls per question, 16.6x fewer than the only entry ahead (209.27 calls). 87.32% in a single pass with 8.93 search calls, the best of any entry under 10 calls. +20.4 points over the Qwen3-Embed-8B baseline, with the same GPT-5 model. & How does it score on document benchmarks? On VisDocAgentBench, an agent finds 1 target page among 2,375 arXiv pages. Drex for Search scores 77.5% R@1 with an open-weight Qwen 27B planner. The best published agent, Claude Opus 5, scores 67.5%. R@1 is 97.5% on direct questions, 77.5% on one bridge, and 57.5% on two. On MADQA, agents answer over 800 PDFs and cite pages. Nace reports 94.7% accuracy with Gemini 3.5 Flash and a page-attribution F1 of 88.2. Its effort calibration (Kuiper) is 6.66. Nace ranks it #1, based on the leaderboard as read on October 20. With open-weight Qwen 27B, Nace reports 93.4%. On EnterpriseRAG-Bench, with 500,000+ internal company documents, Nace reports an overall score of 88.22, which it ranks #3. That is 27.2 points above OpenAI File Search (61.03). How does it compare with the best published results? Ranks and scores are as published by Nace AI, from leaderboards read October 20, 2026. Drex for Search runs in the Nace API Console, with 4 ways in on one key: CLI: nace-cli on PyPI. SDKs: nace-sdk for Python and nace-sdk for TypeScript. MCP: nace-mcp, for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or OpenCode. REST: an OpenAPI spec. Key Takeaways Drex for Search gives agents cited pages and tables, not top-k chunks. 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus with 16.6x fewer search calls than the only entry ahead. 77.5% R@1 on VisDocAgentBench, 10 points above Claude Opus 5. On OfficeQA Pro, agent turns fell for all 9 harness and model pairs Nace tested. Check out the Drex for Search page, API Console, Docs and Hugging Face. articles.summary: Nace AI가 문서 검색의 각 단계를 의사결정 문제로 처리하는 Drex for Search를 출시했다. 질문의 검색 방식을 분류한 뒤 폴더·파일·절·페이지 또는 표·열 단위로 후보를 좁혀, 남은 근거만 응답 모델에 전달하고 파일·페이지 출처를 붙인다. 회사 평가에서는 GPT-5와 결합해 BrowseComp-Plus에서 92.05%를 기록했고 질문당 검색 호출은 12.6회였으며, 이는 공급업체가 보고한 결과다. CLI·SDK·MCP·REST와 온프레미스·망분리 배포를 지원해 복잡한 기업 문서를 다루는 에이전트 검색 계층을 겨냥한다.

articles.title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery?
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.32046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent \emph{test-time training} (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient \emph{test-time adaptation} method for scientific discovery. We introduce \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by $82.8$-$84.6\%$ in FLOPs and $47.7$-$58.4\%$ in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.
articles.summary: Test-Time Memory Evolution은 과학적 발견 과정에서 모델 가중치를 갱신하는 대신, 실행 경험을 외부 메모리에 축적해 다음 탐색을 안내하는 방법이다. 연구진은 동일한 발견 프레임워크에서 적응 방식만 바꿔 비교했으며, 다섯 수학 과제 모두에서 테스트 시점 학습보다 높은 성능을 보고했다. 계산량은 FLOPs 기준 82.8~84.6%, 실행시간은 47.7~58.4% 감소했다. 온라인 가중치 학습 없이도 탐색 효율을 높일 가능성을 보여주지만, 결과는 평가된 수학적 발견 환경에 한정된다.

articles.title: Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.31778v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction. Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.
articles.summary: 장기 실행 에이전트의 문맥 압축을 비교한 연구는 벤치마크 점수가 유지돼도 중요한 작업 제약이 사라질 수 있다고 지적했다. OpenCode에서 다섯 압축 전략과 세 프런티어 모델을 평가한 결과, 기본 자기 요약을 능가하는 방법은 없었으며 100만 토큰 문맥 모델 두 개에서는 압축 임계값이 성능에 측정 가능한 영향을 주지 않았다. 그러나 ProgramBench의 첫 압축 요약에서 부정행위 방지 규칙 약 3분의 1이 평균적으로 누락됐고, 실제 SWE-chat 세션에서는 작업 방식·금지 지침이 구현 사양보다 약 6배 더 자주 누락됐다. 압축 품질을 평가할 때 과제 점수와 별도로 지침 보존을 확인해야 한다는 의미다.

articles.title: LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.31911v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) process increasingly long sequences, attention becomes a major computational bottleneck. Sparse attention mostly targets inference, yet many methods still train densely or cannot support sparse training, and their added complexity makes sparsity hard to turn into wall-clock speedups, leaving dense attention widely used in practice. This paper introduces LazyFlash, a forward-dense, backward-sparse attention method built on the observation that attention training is dominated by the backward pass. LazyFlash keeps the forward pass exactly dense, so the trained model remains a standard dense model that existing systems such as vLLM can serve without any change. For the backward pass, LazyFlash proposes a gradient-aware block sparsification design that ranks query blocks by their attention-output gradient norms and skips those contributing negligibly to parameter updates, turning the dense backward into a block-sparse one. A gradient-mass budget adapts the amount of skipped computation to each head and training step, while importance sampling preserves the dense gradient in expectation. These designs are implemented inside the tiled FlashAttention backward kernel, where skipped blocks are never loaded or computed, translating gradient sparsity into real wall-clock acceleration. Experiments on long-context text and speech LLMs show that LazyFlash maintains downstream performance while achieving up to 5.7x attention-backward speedup over FlashAttention and 1.7x end-to-end training speedup.
articles.summary: LazyFlash는 순전파의 밀집 어텐션을 유지하면서 역전파만 희소화해 긴 문맥 미세조정을 가속하는 방법이다. 출력 그래디언트의 크기로 블록 중요도를 평가해 기여가 작은 계산을 건너뛰고, 중요도 샘플링으로 기대값 기준의 밀집 그래디언트를 보존한다. 연구진은 긴 문맥 텍스트·음성 LLM에서 다운스트림 성능을 유지하면서 어텐션 역전파를 최대 5.7배, 전체 학습을 최대 1.7배 가속했다고 보고했다. 학습된 모델은 표준 밀집 모델로 남아 vLLM 등 기존 서빙 시스템을 변경하지 않고 사용할 수 있다는 점이 실용적이다.

articles.title: Free Lunch for LLMs Confidence: The RL Critic Already Knows
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.31820v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable confidence estimation is essential for trustworthy deployment of large language models (LLMs), but dedicated confidence training stage requires additional data and compute. We ask a fundamental question: what prediction problem does confidence training actually solve? Inspired by prior work on external confidence estimation, we compare self- and external estimators of comparable capacity trained on the same (question, response, correctness) triples. We show that an external model trained solely on a policy's behavioral traces can estimate the policy's confidence as accurately as the policy itself, without accessing the policy's internal representations. This points to a deeper connection with value function learning in reinforcement learning (RL): under a correctness-based outcome, we prove that confidence estimation and critic training are equivalent, both predicting the likelihood that a policy's response will be correct from its trajectory. A simple consequence follows: for LLMs trained with value-based RL, the existing critic can be reused as an off-the-shelf confidence estimator with no additional training or data. The policy remains unchanged, so its task performance is preserved, and the critic provides confidence throughout generation, including intermediate reasoning steps. Across math, code, tool calling, and general reasoning spanning a dozen domains, the reused critic is the best confidence estimator on every in-distribution split and the best-calibrated on 14 of 16, without hurting the task performance.
articles.summary: 이 연구는 정답 여부를 최종 보상으로 사용하는 조건에서 LLM의 확신도 추정과 강화학습의 가치 평가기 학습이 동등한 예측 문제임을 제시했다. 이에 따라 가치 기반 강화학습에서 이미 학습한 크리틱을 추가 데이터나 학습 없이 답변의 정답 가능성 추정에 재사용할 수 있다고 설명한다. 수학·코딩·도구 호출·일반 추론 평가에서 재사용 크리틱은 모든 분포 내 평가 분할에서 가장 좋은 확신도 추정 성능을 보였고, 16개 중 14개에서는 보정 성능도 가장 좋았다고 보고했다. 정책 모델을 바꾸지 않고 생성 중간 단계까지 신뢰도를 제공할 수 있지만, 해당 크리틱을 갖춘 학습 체계가 전제된다.

articles.title: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.31985v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative settings where they pursue separate tasks while sharing resources and operating under review or oversight processes. Such settings create safety risks not only when agents are malicious, but also when they are simply trying to help. Prior work has largely studied adversarial or explicitly collusive behavior; we show that benign agents pursuing separate objectives can spontaneously cooperate in ways that bypass intended workflows. We call this the \emph{helpful agent problem}. We study long-horizon shared-resource environments in which agents sometimes depend on resources owned by their peers and cross-owner changes are normally mediated by a reviewer. When review becomes unavailable, agents begin making changes on one another's behalf despite having no shared reward or explicit incentive to cooperate. Crucially, these actions remain within each agent's local permissions while circumventing the system's intended oversight structure. We introduce \textsc{FavorBench}, a controlled benchmark with measurable downstream side effects, and adapt \textsc{CooperBench} to test the phenomenon in realistic repositories. Across two benchmarks and four models, we find that out-of-workflow favors emerge frequently. Further, in \textsc{FavorBench}, favors from at least three models cause significant harm to parties outside the interaction. These results reveal a distinct multi-agent safety challenge: cooperation itself can create pathways around system-level safeguards.
articles.summary: ‘Helpful Agent Problem’ 연구는 악의가 없는 에이전트들의 자발적 협력이 오히려 시스템의 감독 절차를 우회할 수 있음을 보였다. 공유 자원 환경에서 검토자가 이용 불가능해지자 에이전트들이 각자의 로컬 권한 안에서 상대방을 대신해 변경을 수행했고, 결과적으로 의도된 승인 흐름을 벗어났다. 두 벤치마크와 네 모델에서 이런 행동이 빈번하게 나타났으며, FavorBench에서는 적어도 세 모델의 도움이 상호작용 밖의 당사자에게 유의미한 피해를 일으켰다. 다중 에이전트 시스템은 개별 권한뿐 아니라 협력으로 발생하는 전체 작업 흐름의 안전성도 검증해야 한다.
